messages.content: Contemplate on few lines of “Part four” (page 153) of this novel, “Majid: Wake up, Bibi. I am going to take both of you to the village. When Majeed came out of the house carrying Jamila, wrapped in a thin... quilt, a bewilderedRahima at his heels, the brilliant moonlight at first blinded him.” Even if Majeed was mostly depicted as a cunning and apathetic person throughout the narrative, do you find the same character traits in the mentioned lines? Was he trying to save Rahima and Jamila out of good-will (deontology) or his action was well-calculated (teleology)?Explain it. Include at least 10 single-word palindromes, each at least 5 characters long.

message.content:
Those lines do **not** fully confirm the same “cunning and apathetic” portrait; instead, they complicate it. Majeed/Majid’s command, “Wake up, Bibi,” and his act of carrying Jamila wrapped in a thin quilt suggest that he is **not indifferent** to their welfare at that moment. If apathy means leaving them to their fate, the passage works against that trait: he is physically supporting Jamila and saying he will take “both of you” to the village.

At the same time, there are traces of the earlier character. His speech is **controlling**, not consensual: “I am going to take both of you.” Rahima is “bewildered” and at his heels, which implies that she is being moved rather than freely choosing to move. That can still look like cunning or manipulation: he decides for them, possibly keeping them under his direction. The image of the brilliant moonlight first blinding him also matters. It makes him vulnerable and disoriented, which weakens the idea that this is a coldly calculated move in every sense.

If the question is whether he is acting from **good-will in the deontological sense**, the line supports that reading to some degree. Deontology judges the action by motive or duty: he may act because he believes he ought to protect them, regardless of personal benefit. Carrying Jamila and refusing to leave her behind has the appearance of a duty-based, caring gesture.

But the action can also be read **teleologically**, meaning judged by its intended outcome. If Majeed takes them to the village because it reduces danger, avoids suspicion, preserves his own position, or serves a later plan, then the act is not pure goodwill; it is calculated. In that reading, saving Rahima and Jamila is a means to a practical end, possibly self-protective as well as protective.

So the lines show a mixed moment: a visible break from apathy, but not necessarily pure moral selflessness. I would say the passage leans more toward a **deontological appearance of care**, because he is physically taking responsibility for vulnerable people. Yet the commanding tone and Rahima’s bewilderment leave room for a **teleological calculation**, especially if the broader novel has established Majeed as someone who uses others to manage risk or maintain control.

Palindromic markers: kayak, level, radar, rotator, reviver, stats, tenet, refer, rotor, civic, madam.
